newsitem.title: USA: Cash into stock mutual funds jump in January.
newsitem.headline: Cash into stock mutual funds jump in January.

text.p: After a record-setting 1996, investors opened the new year by pouring a hefty amount of cash into stock and international mutual funds, fund companies said Tuesday.

Fidelity Investments, the nation's largest mutual fund company, said January stock fund sales were off to a strong start, boosted by year-end bonuses and annual corporate payments to employee-sponsored retirement accounts.
"On the domestic equity side, net sales are up significantly from December's levels," Robyn Tice, a spokeswoman for Fidelity, told Reuters.
Net cash inflows into stock mutual funds are expected to "well exceed" $2 billion in January, she said.
"Investors have shown renewed interest in international funds, which are positive this month," she added.
Vanguard Group, which last year for the first time eclipsed Fidelity in the race for new assets, said sales of stock and bond funds hit record levels in January.

"On the equity side alone, last January and last February we took in $2.3 billion each month," Vanguard spokesman Brian Mattes said. "This month, already through yesterday, we've already taken in $2.8 billion."
With a few more days left until February, Mattes said Vanguard expected to take in more than $3 billion into its stock funds for January.
A spokeswoman for Putnam Investments said they also had a strong month of stock mutual fund sales.
"They're still going into growth funds but they're also going into international (funds) and value (funds). There's more broad diversification taking place," she said.

The Investment Company Institute said Tuesday that sales of domestic stock mutual funds across the entire industry slipped in December, the most recent figures available, to $12.22 billion of new cash from $17.16 billion in November.
The December figure was down slightly from an estimate of $13.5 billion made by the industry trade group just over two weeks ago from preliminary figures.
"Early in the month, a lot of investors delayed purchasing until after the funds declared their capital gains distributions," said Chris Wloszczyna, an ICI spokesman.
Most mutual funds declare annual or semi-annual distributions in early December and many investors buy funds later in the month to avoid the tax consequences.
For all of 1996, net new cash flow into stock funds was $222.08 billion, up from $128.22 billion for all of 1995, and easily breaking the record of $129.55 billion in 1993, the ICI said.

Inflows into bond and income funds rose to $2.80 billion in December from $1.43 billion in November due to a new law allowing the tax-free conversion of bank common trusts to mutual funds, Wloszczyna said.
"If you were to factor out these conversions, bond and income funds would have been the same as November," he said.
For the year, flows into bond and income funds were up $13.17 billion after an outflow of $4.81 billion in 1995.

Money market funds had inflows of $3.43 billion in December after a $15.03 billion flood of money in November. For all of 1996, money market funds had a net inflow of $89.32 billion compared with $89.41 billion in 1995.
